stem: A transplant patient taking azathioprine with known intermediate TPMT activity now needs urate-lowering therapy. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Allopurinol at full dose with no change to azathioprine
options.B: Allopurinol with a large azathioprine dose cut and CBC checks
options.C: Probenecid alone, since TPMT status never matters
options.D: Double the azathioprine dose to offset its faster clearance
options.E: No change needed, because TPMT only affects allopurinol

why: Allopurinol raises azathioprine/mercaptopurine exposure (reduce the dose — textbook: by 75%), and low TPMT already raises myelosuppression risk.

whys.A: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which also clears azathioprine.
whys.C: TPMT status always matters for thiopurines.
whys.D: Clearance falls, not rises — marrow toxicity risk climbs.

takeaway: Two hits on thiopurine clearance (TPMT + xanthine oxidase) → cut the dose and watch the CBC.
discriminator: TPMT/NUDT15 = thiopurine genes; HLA-B*58:01 = allopurinol gene.

stem: A patient develops a GI bleed while taking a standard dose of naproxen. How is this adverse effect best classified?

options.A: Toxicity from an overdose above the range
options.B: Type B — idiosyncratic and unpredictable
options.C: Therapeutic effect of reduced inflammation
options.D: Type A — predictable from COX-1 inhibition
options.E: Pharmacogenomic reaction from HLA-B*58:01

why: Blocking COX-1 removes gastric mucosal protection and platelet TXA2 — GI bleeding is a predictable, dose-related extension of the drug’s action (Type A).

whys.A: It occurred at a standard dose.
whys.B: GI injury follows directly from blocking protective prostaglandins.

takeaway: Predictable from the mechanism → Type A.
discriminator: NSAID GI bleed = Type A; allopurinol SJS = Type B.

stem: A patient with osteoporosis has achalasia and cannot stay upright after taking tablets. Which option best addresses both problems?

options.A: Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable
options.B: No therapy, since all osteoporosis drugs are oral
options.C: Weekly oral alendronate with extra water
options.D: Monthly oral ibandronate taken at bedtime
options.E: Crushing the tablet into food

why: Avoid oral bisphosphonates in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright; IV zoledronic acid or an injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.

whys.B: IV and injectable options exist.
whys.C: Achalasia and inability to sit up are contraindications to oral bisphosphonates.
whys.D: Still oral, and lying down raises esophageal risk.
whys.E: Food blocks absorption, and the esophageal problem remains.

takeaway: When the oral route is the problem, change the route.
discriminator: Oral bisphosphonate rules prevent esophageal injury; IV/SC options skip them.

stem: Per the textbook, which instruction about ketorolac is correct?

options.A: Double the dose in patients over 65
options.B: Maximum daily dose is 240 mg
options.C: Use no longer than 5 days
options.D: Start therapy with an oral dose
options.E: Safe long-term in renal impairment

why: Ketorolac is for short-term use only (slides); the textbook adds a 120 mg/day maximum, halved doses in older, light, or renally impaired patients, and no more than 5 days.

whys.A: Doses are halved in patients over 65.
whys.B: The maximum is 120 mg/day.
whys.D: The first dose should be IV or IM (or intranasal), not oral.
whys.E: Doses are halved in renal impairment and use is short-term.

takeaway: Ketorolac: short-term only (≤ 5 days).
discriminator: Short-term ketorolac vs. maintenance NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen.

stem: A 72-year-old with CKD, hypertension, and anticoagulation has an acute gout flare. Which option is often preferred?

options.A: Full-dose colchicine, unadjusted
options.B: A short corticosteroid course
options.C: Probenecid to clear uric acid
options.D: Full-dose oral naproxen
options.E: Starting allopurinol today

why: With these risk factors an oral NSAID is relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred.

whys.A: Colchicine needs renal dose adjustment.
whys.C: Probenecid is avoided in renal impairment.
whys.D: Oral NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated with CKD, anticoagulation, and hypertension.
whys.E: ULT is deferred until the flare resolves.

takeaway: Stacked NSAID red flags in a flare → steroid; adjust colchicine; defer ULT.
discriminator: OA pain in this patient: acetaminophen/topical NSAID; gout flare: short steroid course.

stem: A patient on prednisone 10 mg daily for 2 years asks why bone density is falling. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: Bone loss only happens at doses above 60 mg
options.B: Glucocorticoids raise calcitonin and lower PTH
options.C: More resorption and less bone formation
options.D: Too much osteoblast stimulation by the steroid
options.E: Glucocorticoids block RANKL like denosumab

why: Chronic glucocorticoids increase osteoclast resorption and suppress osteoblast formation (and, per the textbook, cut gut calcium absorption) — a key osteoporosis risk factor.

whys.A: Chronic use at moderate doses is a risk factor.
whys.B: Not the taught mechanism.
whys.D: Formation is suppressed.

takeaway: Chronic steroids → screen and protect bone.
discriminator: Steroid bone loss = more breakdown + less building.

stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis and stage 4 CKD needs baclofen for spasticity. Which plan best reflects safe prescribing?

options.A: Standard dosing, since baclofen is cleared by the liver
options.B: A loading dose to reach steady state faster
options.C: Avoid every centrally acting drug in kidney disease
options.D: Stop it abruptly if any sedation appears
options.E: Use a reduced dose with slow titration and monitor for sedation

why: Baclofen requires renal dose adjustment; reduced clearance raises CNS depression risk, and it must be tapered, not stopped abruptly.

whys.A: Baclofen needs renal dose adjustment.
whys.B: More drug in reduced clearance → CNS depression.
whys.D: Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures and hyperthermia.

takeaway: Renally cleared drug + CKD → lower dose or longer interval, then monitor.
discriminator: Reduce for organ impairment; taper (never stop abruptly) for withdrawal-prone drugs.

stem: A woman with a past DVT asks about raloxifene for osteoporosis. What is the key concern?

options.A: It raises venous thromboembolism risk
options.B: It causes osteonecrosis of the jaw
options.C: It causes rebound vertebral fractures
options.D: It carries a boxed MI and stroke warning
options.E: It must be taken upright with water

why: Raloxifene raises VTE risk (and causes hot flashes), though it may reduce breast cancer risk.

whys.B: A rare bisphosphonate/denosumab effect.
whys.D: That is romosozumab.
whys.E: That is the oral bisphosphonate rule.

takeaway: Raloxifene: clots up, breast cancer risk down.
discriminator: SERM = VTE; romosozumab = MI/stroke.

stem: A patient taking lisinopril and furosemide develops an acute gout flare. Which plan avoids the most predictable kidney injury?

options.A: Avoid an NSAID; treat with a short corticosteroid course
options.B: Start allopurinol today to shorten the flare
options.C: Probenecid to flush uric acid through the kidney
options.D: Full-dose indomethacin for 7 days
options.E: Celecoxib, because COX-2 selectivity spares the kidney

why: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic is the high-yield ‘triple whammy’ AKI pattern; a short corticosteroid course is a good flare alternative when NSAIDs are contraindicated.

whys.B: ULT is deferred until the flare resolves.
whys.C: Chronic ULT, also avoided in renal impairment.
whys.D: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the ‘triple whammy’ for AKI.

takeaway: Check the medication list before choosing a flare drug.
discriminator: Celecoxib protects the stomach, not the kidney.

stem: Which mechanism belongs to baclofen?

options.A: RyR1 blockade in skeletal muscle
options.B: GABA-A facilitation by benzodiazepines
options.C: Central alpha-2 adrenergic agonism
options.D: GABA-B agonism in the spinal cord
options.E: 5-HT2 antagonism in the brainstem

why: Baclofen activates GABA-B receptors, causing presynaptic inhibition and less excitatory transmitter release.

whys.A: That is dantrolene.
whys.B: That is diazepam.

takeaway: Baclofen = GABA-B (B for Baclofen).
discriminator: GABA-B = baclofen; GABA-A = benzodiazepines.

stem: Which statement correctly describes COX-1?

options.A: Enzyme that converts acetaminophen to NAPQI
options.B: Housekeeping enzyme protecting stomach and renal flow
options.C: Main source of inflammatory prostaglandins
options.D: Inducible enzyme found mainly at inflamed sites
options.E: Target of celecoxib's selective inhibition

why: COX-1 is the housekeeping enzyme that maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it contributes to GI and renal adverse effects.

whys.A: Not taught as a COX function.
whys.D: That describes COX-2.

takeaway: COX-1 = housekeeping (GI, kidney). COX-2 = inflammation.
discriminator: Selective COX-2 inhibition spares COX-1, so GI toxicity is lower.

stem: Which effect explains glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis?

options.A: RANKL blockade inside the bone
options.B: Excess calcitonin from the thyroid
options.C: ↑ Osteoblast formation and ↓ resorption
options.D: Excess vitamin D from the kidney
options.E: ↑ Osteoclast resorption and ↓ osteoblast formation

why: Glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven formation, tipping the balance to bone loss.

whys.A: RANKL blockade is denosumab.
whys.B: Not the mechanism taught.
whys.D: Glucocorticoids oppose vitamin D–driven absorption (textbook).

takeaway: Chronic steroids: build less, break more.
discriminator: Steroid-induced osteoporosis is the Session 1 corticosteroid link.

stem: In a gout flare, what activates the inflammatory response once urate crystals form in the joint?

options.A: B cells via CD20 signaling
options.B: Platelets via thromboxane A₂
options.C: Osteoclasts via RANKL signaling
options.D: Neutrophils and macrophages via NLRP3 and IL-1β
options.E: T cells via CD28 costimulation

why: Monosodium urate crystals activate neutrophils and macrophages through NLRP3 and IL-1β, producing the acute flare.

whys.A: CD20 is rituximab’s target in RA.
whys.B: Not the gout cascade taught.
whys.C: RANKL drives bone resorption, not crystal inflammation.
whys.E: Costimulation is abatacept’s target in RA.

takeaway: Crystals → NLRP3/IL-1β → neutrophils → flare.
discriminator: Colchicine blocks the neutrophil step; ULT removes the crystals over time.

stem: A woman in her third trimester asks whether she can take naproxen for back pain. Based on the lecture, what is the best response?

options.A: Use ketorolac daily as a long-term option
options.B: Use it freely — NSAIDs are safest in late pregnancy
options.C: Use celecoxib instead — COX-2 drugs are exempt
options.D: Add folate to make naproxen safe
options.E: Avoid it — late pregnancy is an NSAID caution

why: The lecture lists late pregnancy among the conditions to use NSAIDs with caution or avoid.

whys.A: Ketorolac is for short-term use only.
whys.B: Late pregnancy is on the caution/avoid list.
whys.D: Folate is co-prescribed with methotrexate.

takeaway: NSAID cautions: GI bleed/ulcer, CKD, HF/CV disease, anticoagulants, late pregnancy.
discriminator: Methotrexate is the DMARD contraindicated in pregnancy; NSAIDs are cautioned in late pregnancy.

stem: A patient with RA on adalimumab has a family history of lymphoma and asks about cancer risk. Which statement matches the textbook?

options.A: Boxed warnings apply only to IV biologics
options.B: Only methotrexate carries a malignancy warning
options.C: TNF inhibitors carry a boxed malignancy warning
options.D: Cancer risk applies only to JAK inhibitors
options.E: TNF inhibitors lower lymphoma risk to zero

why: The FDA placed a boxed warning on all anti-TNF agents about possible malignancy, especially lymphoma; periodic skin exams are advised.

whys.A: The warning covers all anti-TNF agents.
whys.B: The boxed malignancy warning is on all anti-TNF agents.
whys.D: JAK inhibitors share a cancer warning, but TNF inhibitors have one too.
whys.E: The FDA boxed warning concerns malignancy, especially lymphoma.

takeaway: TNF inhibitors: infection (TB, hepatitis B) + boxed malignancy warning.
discriminator: TNF boxed = malignancy; JAK boxed = VTE, MACE, cancer.

stem: A patient on long-term colchicine prophylaxis is admitted for pneumonia and started on clarithromycin. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Lower colchicine levels and a breakthrough gout flare
options.B: No meaningful change, since colchicine is renally cleared only
options.C: Colchicine toxicity; reduce or hold colchicine
options.D: Faster uric acid excretion from the antibiotic
options.E: Hemolysis, so check G6PD before continuing

why: CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors (clarithromycin, cyclosporine, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) raise colchicine levels; with its narrow window, toxicity follows.

whys.A: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4/P-gp, so levels rise, not fall.
whys.B: CYP3A4 and P-gp interactions are the taught risk.
whys.D: Not the interaction taught.
whys.E: G6PD screening applies to pegloticase and rasburicase.

takeaway: Narrow-window drug + inhibitor of its clearance → reduce, hold, or switch.
discriminator: Inhibitor → level ↑ (toxicity); inducer → level ↓ (failure).

stem: Falling serum calcium triggers PTH release. Which set lists PTH’s three ways of raising calcium?

options.A: Gut secretion, bone formation, vitamin D breakdown
options.B: Bone formation, renal excretion, gut secretion
options.C: Renal excretion, osteoblast growth, insulin release
options.D: Calcitonin release, bone resorption, sweating
options.E: Bone resorption, renal reabsorption, vitamin D gut absorption

why: PTH raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption.

whys.A: Not the PTH loop.
whys.B: These would lower calcium.
whys.D: Calcitonin opposes PTH.

takeaway: PTH pulls from three: bone, kidney, gut.
discriminator: PTH raises calcium; calcitonin lowers it.

stem: In the OR, a patient develops rising temperature, rigidity, and acidosis after a volatile anesthetic. Which route and drug meet the need for immediate, complete delivery?

options.A: Oral cyclobenzaprine
options.B: Intrathecal baclofen
options.C: Intramuscular botulinum toxin
options.D: Oral dantrolene
options.E: Intravenous dantrolene

why: Malignant hyperthermia is treated with IV dantrolene — IV gives the whole dose at once with no absorption step.

whys.A: A central agent for local spasm.
whys.B: Baclofen treats spasticity, not malignant hyperthermia.
whys.C: Local and slow; not an emergency treatment.
whys.D: Oral absorption is incomplete (about one-third) and too slow for a crisis.

takeaway: Emergency + complete, immediate delivery → IV.
discriminator: Oral dantrolene = chronic spasticity; IV dantrolene = malignant hyperthermia.

stem: A 19-year-old arrives 4 hours after taking a large acetaminophen overdose. Which drug restores the pathway that detoxifies the toxic metabolite?

options.A: N-acetylcysteine
options.B: Folic acid
options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Omeprazole
options.E: Leucovorin

why: Overdose depletes glutathione, so NAPQI accumulates; N-acetylcysteine is a glutathione precursor that replenishes it to detoxify NAPQI.

whys.B: Folate reduces methotrexate toxicity.
whys.C: Naloxone is not taught as an acetaminophen antidote.
whys.D: Not an antidote; used with NSAIDs for GI protection (textbook).

takeaway: Acetaminophen → NAPQI; glutathione detoxifies it; N-acetylcysteine refills glutathione.
discriminator: Folate/leucovorin = methotrexate; N-acetylcysteine = acetaminophen.

stem: A patient’s first gout flare settled two weeks ago; uric acid remains high and flares are recurring. What is the best next step?

options.A: Give colchicine only until the next flare
options.B: Wait for the next flare before deciding
options.C: Start pegloticase as first-line therapy
options.D: Start allopurinol at full dose with no prophylaxis
options.E: Start allopurinol low with colchicine prophylaxis

why: Once the flare resolves, start a xanthine oxidase inhibitor low, titrate to a urate target, and give colchicine or an NSAID prophylaxis for 3–6 months.

whys.A: Recurrent flares with high urate need urate-lowering therapy.
whys.B: The flare has resolved — now is the time to start ULT.
whys.C: Pegloticase is reserved for refractory gout.
whys.D: Start low and cover with colchicine or an NSAID for 3–6 months.

takeaway: ULT starts after the flare, low and slow, with prophylaxis.
discriminator: During a flare: treat the flare. After it: start ULT.

stem: A patient will start infliximab next month and is due for a live vaccine. When should the vaccine be given?

options.A: One week after the first infusion
options.B: Before infliximab is started
options.C: Any time, since biologics don't affect immunity
options.D: Only if a fever develops on therapy
options.E: Never — vaccines are banned for life

why: Update vaccines — especially live vaccines — before starting DMARD therapy, because these drugs suppress the immune response.

whys.A: Live vaccines should be updated before therapy.
whys.D: Fever on therapy needs prompt evaluation for infection, not vaccination.
whys.E: Vaccines are updated before starting, not banned.

takeaway: Vaccinate first, then immunosuppress.
discriminator: Before a biologic: screen (TB, hepatitis B/C) and vaccinate.

stem: What defines a drug as “disease-modifying” in rheumatoid arthritis?

options.A: It selectively blocks the COX-2 isoform
options.B: It relieves pain faster than NSAIDs
options.C: It lowers fever through the hypothalamus
options.D: It is given only as an injection
options.E: It slows or halts joint destruction

why: A DMARD is intended to alter the course of RA — slowing or halting joint destruction and systemic inflammation — rather than only masking symptoms.

whys.A: That is celecoxib, an NSAID.
whys.B: Analgesia alone does not make a drug disease-modifying.
whys.D: Methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs are oral.

takeaway: DMARD = changes the trajectory; NSAID = changes how the patient feels.
discriminator: Ask: does the drug change the disease, or only the symptoms?

stem: Which urate-lowering drug carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death?

options.A: Pegloticase
options.B: Rasburicase
options.C: Allopurinol
options.D: Probenecid
options.E: Febuxostat

why: Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death (the textbook notes later data were reassuring; answer with the slides).

whys.A: Pegloticase’s concerns are G6PD and infusion reactions.
whys.B: Rasburicase’s concern is G6PD deficiency.
whys.D: Probenecid’s concern is kidney stones.

takeaway: Allopurinol = HLA-B*58:01; febuxostat = CV boxed warning.
discriminator: Both are xanthine oxidase inhibitors — the choice turns on safety profile.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes spasticity from rigidity?

options.A: Both respond to the same drugs
options.B: Both follow acute muscle injury
options.C: Spasticity is velocity-dependent; rigidity is not
options.D: Spasticity is a sudden involuntary contraction
options.E: Rigidity is velocity-dependent; spasticity is not

why: Spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone from upper motor neuron injury; rigidity is constant tone, independent of velocity.

whys.A: They often need distinct approaches.
whys.B: Spasm follows injury; spasticity is upper motor neuron.
whys.D: That describes muscle spasm.

takeaway: Spasticity speeds up with speed; rigidity doesn’t care.
discriminator: Spasm = sudden contraction after injury; spasticity = UMN; rigidity = constant.

stem: A 70-year-old with a stroke 8 months ago has very high fracture risk. Which anabolic choice is most defensible?

options.A: No anabolic agent, since all carry a stroke warning
options.B: Raloxifene, which is the strongest anabolic drug
options.C: Romosozumab, since it both builds bone and limits resorption
options.D: Teriparatide or abaloparatide rather than romosozumab
options.E: Calcitonin alone as the first-line anabolic

why: Romosozumab carries a boxed warning for MI, stroke, and CV death (textbook: contraindicated after MI or stroke within a year); the PTH analogs are the anabolic alternative (2-year limit).

whys.A: Only romosozumab carries it.
whys.B: Raloxifene is antiresorptive, and it raises VTE risk.
whys.C: Its boxed warning (MI, stroke, CV death) applies here.

takeaway: A boxed warning that matches the patient’s history steers you to the alternative.
discriminator: Anabolic: teriparatide/abaloparatide (2 years) vs romosozumab (CV boxed warning).

stem: Before starting adalimumab, a patient’s interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most appropriate decision?

options.A: Give a live vaccine first to boost immunity
options.B: Treat latent TB before starting the TNF inhibitor
options.C: Switch to methotrexate daily instead
options.D: Avoid every DMARD permanently
options.E: Start adalimumab now; TB screening is a formality

why: All DMARDs share infection risk; screen for TB and hepatitis B/C and update vaccines before starting a biologic, treating positives first.

whys.A: Live vaccines are avoided around immunosuppression.
whys.C: Methotrexate is weekly; and TB still needs treatment.
whys.D: An absolute not taught.

takeaway: Screen → treat → then start the biologic.
discriminator: Biologic risk = infection; fever on a biologic = infection until proven otherwise.

stem: Ten days after starting allopurinol, a patient develops a rash and fever. A severe cutaneous reaction is suspected. How is this reaction best classified?

options.A: Type B (idiosyncratic) reaction — stop allopurinol at once
options.B: Toxicity from levels above the therapeutic range
options.C: Expected therapeutic effect of lowering uric acid
options.D: Type A (augmented) reaction — lower the dose and continue
options.E: A drug–drug interaction with prophylactic colchicine

why: Allopurinol hypersensitivity (SJS/TEN, linked to HLA-B*58:01) is unpredictable and not dose-related; the textbook says stop at the first sign of a rash.

whys.B: It occurs at normal doses; risk is genetic (HLA-B*58:01).
whys.C: A rash is unintended and harmful.
whys.D: Not a dose-related extension of xanthine oxidase inhibition.

takeaway: Unpredictable, immune/genetic, not dose-related = Type B; stop the drug.
discriminator: Type A = predictable extension of the drug’s action; Type B = idiosyncratic.

stem: Denosumab has controlled a patient’s osteoporosis for 5 years. The patient now wants to stop all injections. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Improved bone density once the antibody clears
options.B: Rebound vertebral fractures unless a bisphosphonate follows
options.C: No change, since its effect persists in bone for years
options.D: Malignant hyperthermia during later surgery
options.E: Hypercalcemia that requires saline diuresis

why: Denosumab blocks osteoclast formation without killing osteoclasts or depositing in bone; stopping causes rebound resorption and vertebral fractures — transition to a bisphosphonate.

whys.A: Resorption surges after stopping.
whys.D: Unrelated.

takeaway: Reversible antiresorptive → plan the handoff before stopping.
discriminator: Bisphosphonate = long skeletal half-life (holiday possible); denosumab = rebound if stopped.

stem: A 76-year-old with benign prostatic hyperplasia asks for a muscle relaxant for a back strain. Why is cyclobenzaprine a poor fit?

options.A: It causes hemolysis in older adults with BPH
options.B: Anticholinergic effects: urinary retention, confusion
options.C: It requires routine liver enzyme monitoring with use
options.D: It blocks RyR1 and causes profound weakness
options.E: It is only effective given intrathecally

why: Cyclobenzaprine is tricyclic-like: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion — on the Beers list for older adults.

whys.A: Not a taught effect.
whys.C: LFT monitoring is emphasized for tizanidine.
whys.D: That is dantrolene.

takeaway: Older adult + anticholinergic burden → think Beers list.
discriminator: Cyclobenzaprine = anticholinergic; tizanidine = hypotension/LFTs; baclofen = sedation/withdrawal.

stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use who has barely eaten for days takes acetaminophen at the upper end of normal dosing. Why is their liver risk higher?

options.A: Alcohol converts acetaminophen into an NSAID
options.B: Fasting saturates TXA2, causing hepatic bleeding
options.C: Lower glutathione plus induced CYP2E1 makes more NAPQI
options.D: Fasting speeds renal excretion of the parent drug
options.E: Alcohol blocks COX in the liver, adding NSAID toxicity

why: Chronic alcohol use and fasting lower glutathione (GSH) and both induce CYP2E1, so more drug becomes NAPQI and less can be neutralized.

whys.A: Not taught; acetaminophen is not an NSAID.
whys.B: TXA2 relates to NSAIDs and platelets.
whys.D: Fasting lowers glutathione; it doesn't explain liver risk via kidneys.
whys.E: The taught mechanism is glutathione and CYP2E1, not COX.

takeaway: Alcohol + fasting: ↓ GSH, ↑ CYP2E1 → more NAPQI.
discriminator: Safe route (~90%) = glucuronidation/sulfation; risky route (~5–10%) = CYP2E1 → NAPQI.

stem: A patient stable on tizanidine for spasticity is prescribed fluvoxamine. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Avoid the pair — CYP1A2 inhibition raises tizanidine
options.B: Continue both, since tizanidine has a wide therapeutic index
options.C: Increase the tizanidine dose to keep spasticity controlled
options.D: Check G6PD before starting fluvoxamine
options.E: Switch tizanidine to an IV form to bypass the interaction

why: Ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine strongly inhibit CYP1A2, raising tizanidine levels (hypotension, sedation) — the combination is contraindicated.

whys.B: The combination is contraindicated.
whys.C: Levels rise; more drug worsens hypotension and sedation.
whys.D: Not the interaction taught.
whys.E: No IV form is taught; the issue is metabolism.

takeaway: Know each drug’s metabolizing enzyme: tizanidine = CYP1A2.
discriminator: Colchicine = CYP3A4/P-gp; tizanidine = CYP1A2.

stem: A pharmacist calls: a new prescription reads “methotrexate 15 mg by mouth daily” for RA. What is the safety problem?

options.A: It should be IV only in RA
options.B: It needs N-acetylcysteine with each dose
options.C: It should be weekly; daily dosing can be fatal
options.D: It should be twice daily for steady levels
options.E: Nothing — daily dosing is standard for RA

why: Methotrexate is dosed weekly, not daily — a critical patient-safety point, since daily dosing can be fatal.

whys.A: The dosing error is frequency, not route.
whys.B: Folate, not N-acetylcysteine, is co-prescribed.
whys.D: Methotrexate for RA is weekly.
whys.E: Daily dosing is the dangerous error.

takeaway: Methotrexate: weekly + folate.
discriminator: The one RA drug where frequency errors kill.

stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on celecoxib for osteoarthritis. What should the clinician anticipate?

options.A: Hemolysis requiring G6PD testing
options.B: No change, since celecoxib spares platelets
options.C: Faster renal clearance of warfarin
options.D: Lower INR and clot formation
options.E: Higher bleeding risk — monitor INR closely

why: NSAIDs plus anticoagulants raise bleeding risk; the textbook adds that celecoxib (a CYP2C9 substrate) occasionally interacts with warfarin.

whys.A: Unrelated.
whys.B: NSAIDs plus anticoagulants still raise bleeding risk.
whys.D: Celecoxib does not reduce warfarin effect.

takeaway: Anticoagulant + any NSAID → anticipate bleeding and monitor.
discriminator: Celecoxib lowers GI ulcer risk but not interaction risk.

stem: A 22-year-old took a single large acetaminophen ingestion at a known time; a level drawn 8 hours later is 120 mcg/mL. Using the lecture's nomogram, what is the next step?

options.A: Discharge: levels fall below 150 by 8 hours
options.B: Ignore the level and treat with an NSAID
options.C: Wait until 24 hours for a second level first
options.D: Repeat the level before 4 hours have passed
options.E: Start NAC: the level is above the treatment line

why: On the Rumack-Matthew nomogram the slide's example — 8 h, 120 mcg/mL — is above the treatment line, so NAC is started (give early for best effect).

whys.A: At 8 hours the treatment line is 75 mcg/mL; 120 is above it.
whys.B: NSAIDs don't treat acetaminophen toxicity.
whys.C: The slide's example says start NAC; delay worsens outcome.
whys.D: Levels before 4 hours can't be plotted; this one is at 8 hours.

takeaway: Single acute ingestion, level at ≥ 4 h: above the line → NAC; below → toxicity unlikely.
discriminator: Not valid before 4 h, after 24 h, or for chronic/staggered ingestion: use AST/ALT and poison control.

stem: What distinguishes dantrolene from cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, and baclofen?

options.A: It acts on the muscle fiber, not the CNS
options.B: It is a central alpha-2 agonist
options.C: It acts in the brainstem on 5-HT2
options.D: It blocks ACh release at the junction
options.E: It acts on GABA-B receptors in the cord

why: Dantrolene decreases calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (RyR1) inside the muscle fiber; the others act in the CNS.

whys.B: That is tizanidine.
whys.D: That is botulinum toxin.

takeaway: Dantrolene = the only muscle-side relaxant.
discriminator: Central: baclofen, tizanidine, cyclobenzaprine. Peripheral: dantrolene (muscle), botulinum (junction).

stem: Which drug lowers serum uric acid by increasing its renal excretion?

options.A: Colchicine
options.B: Pegloticase
options.C: Probenecid
options.D: Febuxostat
options.E: Allopurinol

why: Probenecid is a uricosuric: it blocks URAT1-mediated tubular reabsorption, so excretion rises.

whys.A: Colchicine calms inflammation; it does not lower uric acid.
whys.B: Pegloticase breaks uric acid down to allantoin.
whys.D: Febuxostat also inhibits xanthine oxidase.
whys.E: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering production.

takeaway: Make less (xanthine oxidase inhibitors), pee more (probenecid), break it down (uricase).
discriminator: Uricosuric = ↑ excretion; xanthine oxidase inhibitor = ↓ production.

stem: Which osteoporosis drug is limited to 2 years of lifetime use and should be followed by an antiresorptive?

options.A: Alendronate
options.B: Denosumab
options.C: Raloxifene
options.D: Teriparatide
options.E: Zoledronic acid

why: Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then followed by an antiresorptive to keep the bone gained.

whys.A: Bisphosphonates get a drug holiday after 3–5 years.
whys.B: Denosumab must not simply be stopped.
whys.E: Given yearly IV; no 2-year cap taught.

takeaway: Build (teriparatide 2 years), then keep (antiresorptive).
discriminator: Teriparatide = time limit; denosumab = no abrupt stop; romosozumab = CV boxed warning.

stem: Which sequence describes joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis, as opposed to osteoarthritis?

options.A: Uric acid crystals deposit and trigger a flare
options.B: Synovitis forms a pannus; TNF-α and IL-6 drive erosion
options.C: Mechanical wear degrades cartilage; osteophytes form
options.D: NAPQI binds proteins in the synovial lining
options.E: Prostaglandin loss thins the gastric mucosa

why: RA is autoimmune: immune activation causes synovitis with pannus formation that erodes cartilage and bone, with TNF-α and IL-6 driving inflammation and damage — the cytokines biologics target.

whys.A: Gout is taught in Session 2, not RA.
whys.D: NAPQI is acetaminophen's toxic metabolite.

takeaway: OA = mechanical wear → cartilage loss → osteophytes. RA = immune synovitis → pannus → TNF-α/IL-6 erosion.
discriminator: The RA cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) are exactly what TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab block.

stem: A pharmacy label reads ‘methotrexate 15 mg by mouth daily’ for a new RA patient. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Dispense it — daily dosing gives faster control
options.B: Switch to IV methotrexate to bypass first-pass
options.C: Dispense it but halve the dose
options.D: Hold it; correct to once weekly with folate
options.E: Add an NSAID to protect the liver from toxicity

why: Methotrexate for RA is weekly only — daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity — with folate co-prescribed.

whys.A: Daily dosing has caused fatal toxicity.
whys.B: The problem is the daily schedule.
whys.C: The error is the frequency, not only the dose.

takeaway: Methotrexate: weekly, with folate, never in pregnancy.
discriminator: Weekly methotrexate vs daily for every other DMARD taught.

stem: Why is celecoxib associated with more cardiovascular events than its GI profile would suggest?

options.A: It depletes glutathione in the heart
options.B: It raises renal blood flow excessively
options.C: TXA2 falls while PGI2 is preserved
options.D: PGI2 falls while platelet TXA2 is preserved
options.E: It blocks COX-1 more than COX-2

why: Celecoxib blocks COX-2, lowering prostacyclin (PGI2) without a matching drop in platelet thromboxane (TXA2, made by spared COX-1) — the balance tips toward clotting.

whys.A: Glutathione depletion is acetaminophen overdose.
whys.B: NSAIDs lower renal blood flow; the kidney is still affected.

takeaway: Celecoxib: GI ↓ (COX-1 spared), CV ↑ (PGI2 ↓, TXA2 kept), kidney still affected.
discriminator: Nonselective NSAIDs lower TXA2 too (bleeding risk); celecoxib does not.

stem: A patient on tizanidine reports dizziness on standing and has new elevated liver enzymes. Which pair of effects is typical of tizanidine?

options.A: Anticholinergic retention and confusion
options.B: Hemolysis and infusion reactions
options.C: Hypotension and hepatotoxicity
options.D: Hyperkalemia and fasciculations
options.E: Esophagitis and hypocalcemia

why: Tizanidine causes sedation, hypotension/bradycardia, dry mouth, and hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs.

whys.A: Typical of cyclobenzaprine.
whys.B: Typical of pegloticase.
whys.D: Typical of succinylcholine.

takeaway: Tizanidine: low BP, sleepy, dry, check LFTs.
discriminator: Tizanidine = α2 effects + liver; cyclobenzaprine = anticholinergic.

stem: A patient takes 4 g of acetaminophen daily plus a nightly cold-and-flu product, and drinks alcohol heavily. Three weeks later, AST and ALT are markedly elevated. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.A: Continue and repeat liver tests in six months
options.B: Stop all acetaminophen and work up liver injury
options.C: Switch to an NSAID-acetaminophen combination
options.D: Double the acetaminophen dose to control the pain
options.E: Ignore it — acetaminophen is safe at any dose

why: Hidden acetaminophen in combination products plus chronic alcohol use (↓ glutathione, ↑ CYP2E1) raises NAPQI injury risk; stop the suspected drug and work up liver injury.

whys.A: Delaying risks serious liver harm.
whys.D: More drug means more NAPQI.

takeaway: New liver injury on a hepatotoxic drug → stop it and investigate.
discriminator: Alcohol and fasting raise acetaminophen toxicity risk.

stem: A patient with heart failure on furosemide develops worsening edema after starting high-dose ibuprofen. What best explains this?

options.A: Ibuprofen is a CYP inducer lowering furosemide
options.B: The edema is NAPQI-induced liver failure
options.C: Ibuprofen is COX-2 selective and hurts the heart
options.D: NSAIDs cause fluid retention and blunt diuretics
options.E: Furosemide blocks ibuprofen's COX inhibition

why: NSAIDs cause renal fluid retention and, with diuretics, reduce the diuretic effect and raise renal risk; heart failure is a caution for NSAID use.

whys.A: Not the taught mechanism; NSAIDs reduce diuretic effect directly.
whys.B: NAPQI comes from acetaminophen.
whys.E: The interaction runs the other way.

takeaway: NSAID + diuretic → less diuresis, more renal risk.
discriminator: NSAID + anticoagulant = bleeding; + ACEi/ARB (+ diuretic) = AKI; + steroid = ulcer.

stem: A trial shows a weekly bisphosphonate prevents fractures, but in practice many patients miss doses because of the strict fasting rules. What does this gap illustrate?

options.A: Poor bioavailability, which IV dosing cannot fix
options.B: The difference between efficacy and effectiveness
options.C: The difference between potency and efficacy
options.D: A Type B adverse drug reaction
options.E: Drug tolerance from long skeletal half-life

why: Efficacy is performance under trial conditions; effectiveness is real-world performance with adherence — dosing frequency drives which bisphosphonate patients actually take.

whys.A: IV dosing bypasses absorption entirely.
whys.C: Potency is dose needed; this is trial vs real-world use.
whys.D: Missed doses are an adherence problem, not an ADR.

takeaway: Trial results set the ceiling; adherence decides real-world benefit.
discriminator: Efficacy (ideal conditions) vs effectiveness (real world).

stem: A 58-year-old with a prior bleeding ulcer and a recent myocardial infarction needs an anti-inflammatory. Why is celecoxib not a simple solution?

options.A: It raises GI risk but lowers cardiovascular risk
options.B: It has no effect on inflammatory prostaglandins
options.C: It lowers GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk
options.D: It is an antidote, not an anti-inflammatory
options.E: It protects the kidney but harms the liver

why: COX-2 selectivity gives a lower ulcer/bleeding risk but is associated with more cardiovascular events; renal risk is unchanged.

whys.A: Reversed: celecoxib lowers GI risk and raises CV risk.
whys.B: It blocks COX-2, the main source of them.
whys.D: Celecoxib is a COX-2 selective NSAID.
whys.E: Renal risk is similar to nonselective NSAIDs.

takeaway: Celecoxib: GI ↓, CV ↑, kidney =.
discriminator: There is no risk-free NSAID — only a different risk profile.

stem: Which non-drug approaches does the lecture include in osteoarthritis management?

options.A: Activity modification, physical therapy, weight management
options.B: Glutathione replenishment, label review
options.C: Fasting, high-protein diet, bed rest
options.D: Live vaccines, TB screening, folate
options.E: Nerve ablation, spinal cord stimulation

why: OA management includes activity modification, physical therapy, and weight management alongside drugs.

whys.B: These relate to acetaminophen.
whys.D: These are DMARD safety steps.

takeaway: OA = pain control and function, drug and non-drug.
discriminator: OA goals vs. RA goals.

stem: A patient with RA cannot tolerate methotrexate. Which conventional DMARD does the lecture name as the alternative?

options.A: Leflunomide
options.B: Rituximab
options.C: Sulfasalazine
options.D: Celecoxib
options.E: Hydroxychloroquine

why: Leflunomide is the alternative when methotrexate is not tolerated.

whys.B: A biologic, not a conventional DMARD.
whys.C: Named as often used in combinations.
whys.D: An NSAID, not a DMARD.

takeaway: Methotrexate anchor · HCQ milder · sulfasalazine combos · leflunomide if MTX not tolerated.
discriminator: Conventional (small molecule) vs. biologic DMARDs.

stem: A patient with gout and a history of uric acid kidney stones needs urate-lowering therapy. Which drug should be avoided?

options.A: Allopurinol
options.B: Prednisone
options.C: Colchicine
options.D: Probenecid
options.E: Febuxostat

why: Probenecid raises urinary uric acid, so avoid it with uric acid kidney stones or significant renal impairment.

whys.A: Allopurinol lowers production and is first-line.
whys.B: Prednisone treats flares; it does not raise urinary urate.
whys.C: Colchicine is a flare/prophylaxis drug, not the stone concern.
whys.E: Febuxostat lowers production; its concern is CV.

takeaway: Uricosurics load the urine with urate: no stones, hydrate well.
discriminator: Probenecid: kidney stones and renal impairment are the stop signs.

stem: Which sequence describes how tissue injury produces musculoskeletal pain?

options.A: Injury → glutathione loss → NAPQI build-up → pain
options.B: Injury → COX-1 induction → gastric protection → pain
options.C: Injury → nerve transection → cortical atrophy → pain
options.D: Injury → mediator release → nociceptor sensitization → pain
options.E: Injury → T-cell depletion → B-cell surge → pain

why: Tissue injury releases inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) that sensitize nociceptors, producing pain.

whys.A: That chain is acetaminophen overdose.
whys.B: COX-1 is housekeeping; COX-2 is the inducible inflammatory isoform.
whys.C: Nerve injury is neuropathic pain, not the lecture's inflammatory cascade.

takeaway: Mediators sensitize nociceptors: that is why blocking prostaglandin synthesis relieves inflammatory pain.
discriminator: Neuropathic = nerve damage; nociceptive/inflammatory = mediators acting on receptors.

stem: Which drug blocks osteoclast formation by inhibiting RANKL?

options.A: Denosumab
options.B: Teriparatide
options.C: Alendronate
options.D: Romosozumab
options.E: Raloxifene

why: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that blocks osteoclast formation (it mimics OPG).

whys.B: Teriparatide is an anabolic PTH analog.
whys.C: Alendronate causes osteoclast apoptosis via FPP synthase.
whys.D: Romosozumab targets sclerostin.

takeaway: Denosumab = RANKL; romosozumab = sclerostin.
discriminator: Both are -sumab bone antibodies; know the target.

stem: A prescription reads infliximab. What does the stem “-ximab” tell you?

options.A: A kinase inhibitor
options.B: A fully human monoclonal antibody
options.C: A humanized monoclonal antibody
options.D: A receptor fusion protein
options.E: A chimeric monoclonal antibody

why: -ximab marks a chimeric antibody; infliximab is a chimeric anti-TNF-α antibody.

whys.A: Kinase inhibitors end in -nib/-tinib (tofacitinib).
whys.B: Fully human antibodies end in -umab (adalimumab).
whys.D: Fusion proteins end in -cept (etanercept, abatacept).

takeaway: -zumab humanized · -ximab chimeric · -umab fully human · -cept fusion · -tinib kinase.
discriminator: Read the stem first: it reveals the class before you recall the drug.

stem: A patient starting weekly risedronate asks how to take it. Which instruction is correct?

options.A: With an antacid to protect the stomach
options.B: At bedtime, then lie down to rest
options.C: With coffee to help it absorb
options.D: With breakfast and a calcium tablet
options.E: Fasting, full glass of water, upright 30 minutes

why: Take it first thing in the morning, fasting, with a full glass of plain water, and stay upright for 30 minutes to limit esophageal irritation.

whys.A: Antacids reduce absorption.
whys.B: Lying down raises esophageal risk.
whys.D: Food and calcium cut absorption.

takeaway: Oral bisphosphonates: empty stomach, full glass of water, upright.
discriminator: Absorption is under 1% — anything else in the stomach cuts it further.

stem: A transplant patient taking azathioprine develops gout and needs allopurinol. What must happen?

options.A: Switch the allopurinol to colchicine
options.B: No change; there is no interaction
options.C: Reduce the azathioprine dose substantially
options.D: Stop azathioprine for one week
options.E: Double the azathioprine dose

why: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, which clears azathioprine and mercaptopurine — reduce their dose (textbook: by 75%).

whys.A: Colchicine doesn’t lower uric acid.
whys.B: Xanthine oxidase also clears azathioprine.
whys.D: The fix is a dose reduction (textbook: by 75%).
whys.E: Allopurinol raises azathioprine levels, not lowers them.

takeaway: Allopurinol + azathioprine/mercaptopurine → cut the thiopurine dose.
discriminator: Colchicine’s interaction is CYP3A4/P-gp; allopurinol’s is the thiopurines.

stem: Which effect is acetaminophen least reliable for?

options.A: Pain in a patient with CKD
options.B: Relieving mild-to-moderate pain
options.C: Lowering fever
options.D: Reducing peripheral inflammation
options.E: First-line mild osteoarthritis pain

why: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever centrally, but its peripheral anti-inflammatory effect is minimal.

whys.A: It is generally safer than an NSAID with kidney disease.
whys.B: Acetaminophen is an effective analgesic.
whys.C: It is antipyretic via the hypothalamic temperature center.
whys.E: It is a reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.

takeaway: Pain + fever: yes. Inflammation: no.
discriminator: Need an anti-inflammatory → NSAID; need analgesia with NSAID red flags → acetaminophen.

stem: Three weeks after starting methotrexate for RA, a patient wants to stop it because the joints still ache. What is the best response?

options.A: Switch to daily dosing to speed the response
options.B: Continue: DMARD protection builds over weeks to months
options.C: Stop it — a DMARD that works relieves pain within days
options.D: Replace it with an NSAID to change the disease course
options.E: Add acetaminophen instead, since RA is degenerative

why: NSAIDs relieve symptoms in days, while DMARDs protect joints over weeks to months; DMARDs modify the disease course rather than just masking symptoms.

whys.A: Methotrexate is weekly only; daily dosing has been fatal.
whys.C: Fast relief in days is the NSAID pattern, not the DMARD one.
whys.D: NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not modify RA.
whys.E: RA is autoimmune; OA is degenerative.

takeaway: DMARDs are slow but change the disease; bridge symptoms, don’t abandon the DMARD.
discriminator: NSAID = fast symptom relief; DMARD = slow disease modification.

stem: Which drug is a TNF inhibitor?

options.A: Etanercept
options.B: Leflunomide
options.C: Rituximab
options.D: Tocilizumab
options.E: Abatacept

why: Adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab are the lecture's TNF inhibitors.

whys.B: A conventional DMARD.
whys.D: An IL-6 inhibitor.

takeaway: TNF: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
discriminator: TNF · IL-6 (tocilizumab) · B cell (rituximab) · T-cell costimulation (abatacept).

stem: A 68-year-old woman with prior vertebral fractures and very high fracture risk is choosing therapy. What does the lecture suggest first?

options.A: Calcium and vitamin D alone
options.B: Calcitonin nasal spray
options.C: An anabolic agent such as teriparatide
options.D: A drug holiday from all therapy
options.E: Raloxifene for hip protection

why: Higher-risk patients may need an anabolic agent first (then an antiresorptive); fracture history, renal function, and route also guide choice.

whys.A: Supportive, but not enough at very high risk.
whys.B: Calcitonin is a weaker antiresorptive.
whys.D: Holidays apply after years of bisphosphonate.
whys.E: Raloxifene protects the spine, not the hip (textbook).

takeaway: Very high fracture risk → anabolic first, antiresorptive after.
discriminator: Anabolic: teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumab. Antiresorptive: bisphosphonates, denosumab, SERMs, calcitonin.

stem: Which drug pairing does the lecture flag for a higher GI ulcer risk?

options.A: NSAID plus a corticosteroid
options.B: Acetaminophen plus N-acetylcysteine
options.C: NSAID plus an anticoagulant
options.D: NSAID plus a diuretic
options.E: NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor

why: NSAIDs combined with corticosteroids raise GI ulcer risk.

whys.B: That is overdose treatment.
whys.D: That pairing reduces diuretic effect and raises renal risk.

takeaway: Steroid + NSAID = ulcer.
discriminator: Match each NSAID interaction to its organ: blood, kidney, kidney, stomach.

stem: In the OR, after sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a patient’s end-tidal CO₂ and temperature climb with jaw rigidity. Which drug is given IV now?

options.A: Tizanidine
options.B: Neostigmine
options.C: Baclofen
options.D: Dantrolene
options.E: Cyclobenzaprine

why: Malignant hyperthermia (volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine) is treated with IV dantrolene, which blocks RyR1 calcium release.

whys.A: Tizanidine is an oral central agent.
whys.B: Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing blockers.

takeaway: MH → IV dantrolene, now.
discriminator: Dantrolene also treats neuroleptic malignant syndrome; MH triggers are volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine.

stem: Which NSAID is noted for oral and topical formulations?

options.A: Naproxen
options.B: Diclofenac
options.C: Celecoxib
options.D: Ketorolac
options.E: Indomethacin

why: Diclofenac is available in oral and topical formulations; topical NSAIDs give local relief with much lower systemic exposure.

whys.A: Noted for its longer half-life and twice-daily dosing.
whys.D: Noted for short-term use and GI/renal risk.
whys.E: Noted as more potent with more GI/CNS effects.

takeaway: Topical NSAID = local relief, much lower systemic exposure.
discriminator: Ibuprofen first-line · naproxen twice daily · diclofenac topical · indomethacin potent · ketorolac short-term.

stem: A patient using acetaminophen for back pain also takes a nighttime sleep aid and a cold-and-flu product. What should the PA do first?

options.A: Review every product label for hidden acetaminophen
options.B: Switch the back-pain drug to celecoxib at once
options.C: Reassure that OTC products are always safe
options.D: Check a creatinine for NSAID renal injury
options.E: Add N-acetylcysteine as routine prevention

why: Many combination cold, flu, and sleep products contain acetaminophen; unintentional double-dosing is a leading cause of acetaminophen liver injury, so ask about all sources.

whys.B: The problem is a hidden second source of acetaminophen, not the choice of analgesic.
whys.C: Combination products are a leading cause of unintentional double-dosing.
whys.D: None of the products described is an NSAID.
whys.E: N-acetylcysteine is the overdose antidote, not routine prophylaxis.

takeaway: Always ask about ALL sources of acetaminophen.
discriminator: Hidden duplication (same ingredient, two products) vs. drug interaction (two different drugs).

stem: A patient with gout, a recent myocardial infarction, and a mild rash on allopurinol needs a different urate-lowering drug. Why is febuxostat a cautious choice?

options.A: Its boxed CV-death warning, weighed against alternatives
options.B: It is a uricosuric that causes uric acid kidney stones
options.C: It works only during an acute flare
options.D: It cannot lower uric acid at all in any kidney disease
options.E: It must never be combined with any other drug

why: Febuxostat is the alternative when allopurinol isn’t tolerated, but it carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death — a risk–benefit judgment against other options.

whys.B: Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
whys.D: Textbook: it appears safe in moderate CKD.

takeaway: Risk–benefit is comparative: weigh a boxed warning against the alternatives available.
discriminator: Allopurinol = HLA-B*58:01; febuxostat = CV boxed warning.

stem: Rituximab treats rheumatoid arthritis by which mechanism?

options.A: Blocking TNF-α signaling
options.B: Blocking IL-6 receptor signaling
options.C: Blocking T-cell costimulation
options.D: Depleting or modulating B lymphocytes
options.E: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase

why: Rituximab is B-cell targeted therapy: it depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.

whys.A: That is adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab.
whys.B: That is tocilizumab.

takeaway: Rituximab → B cells.
discriminator: Each biologic class hits a different cell or cytokine in the cascade.

stem: Which set lists methotrexate's key adverse effects from the lecture?

options.A: Retinopathy, cardiomyopathy, myopathy
options.B: Hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity
options.C: Hypersensitivity, lymphoma, heart failure
options.D: GI bleeding, AKI, cardiovascular events
options.E: Tinnitus, aseptic meningitis, rash

why: Methotrexate's key adverse effects are hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, and pulmonary toxicity; folate reduces toxicity.

whys.A: Those are antimalarial (hydroxychloroquine) toxicities in the textbook.
whys.C: TNF-inhibitor themes, not methotrexate's taught list.
whys.D: That is the NSAID triad.

takeaway: Methotrexate hits liver, marrow, lung.
discriminator: NSAIDs: gut, kidney, heart. Methotrexate: liver, marrow, lung.

stem: A 45-year-old has symmetric hand-joint swelling, morning stiffness, and a positive rheumatoid factor. Why are NSAIDs alone not enough?

options.A: RA pain is neuropathic and needs nerve blockers
options.B: RA is degenerative, so only steroid injections work
options.C: NSAIDs have no analgesic effect in any arthritis
options.D: RA needs disease-modifying therapy, not pain relief alone
options.E: NSAIDs are contraindicated in everyone with RA

why: RA is an autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease whose goal is to suppress disease activity; NSAIDs ease symptoms without altering the disease course.

whys.A: RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease.
whys.B: RA is autoimmune; OA is degenerative.
whys.C: NSAIDs relieve symptoms; they just don't change the disease course.
whys.E: Not taught; the issue is that they don't modify the disease.

takeaway: OA → pain control and function; RA → suppress disease activity with DMARDs.
discriminator: Degenerative (OA) vs. immune-mediated (RA).
src: L03 S41; S41 (notes); S45 (notes); p. 676; p. 701

stem: Why do corticosteroids suppress a broader range of inflammatory mediators than NSAIDs?

options.A: They neutralize TNF-α outside the cell
options.B: They deplete B cells that release prostaglandins
options.C: They block phospholipase A₂, upstream of COX
options.D: They block COX-2 more strongly than any NSAID
options.E: They act centrally on the hypothalamus

why: Corticosteroids block phospholipase A₂, preventing arachidonic acid release, so a broad range of mediators falls; NSAIDs act only at COX.

whys.A: That is the TNF-inhibitor mechanism.
whys.B: B-cell depletion is rituximab.
whys.D: Corticosteroids act upstream at phospholipase A₂, not at COX.

takeaway: Upstream block (phospholipase A₂) = broad effect; COX block = prostaglandins only.
discriminator: Corticosteroid → phospholipase A₂; NSAID/coxib → COX.

stem: A patient from a region with high tuberculosis rates is about to start adalimumab. Which step matters most before the first dose?

options.A: Check a uric acid level
options.B: Obtain a baseline eye examination
options.C: Review labels for hidden acetaminophen
options.D: Start folate supplementation
options.E: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B/C

why: Immunosuppression is the shared DMARD risk; baseline TB and hepatitis B/C screening comes before biologics (TNF inhibitors can reactivate TB and hepatitis B).

whys.A: Not a biologic safety step.
whys.B: Eye exams apply to hydroxychloroquine (textbook).
whys.D: Folate accompanies methotrexate.

takeaway: Biologic start: TB + hepatitis screen, vaccines first.
discriminator: Shared DMARD risk = infection.

stem: A patient taking sertraline is prescribed cyclobenzaprine for a back strain. What interaction should the PA flag?

options.A: Rebound spasticity
options.B: Serotonin syndrome
options.C: Malignant hyperthermia
options.D: Hemolytic anemia
options.E: Acute kidney injury

why: Cyclobenzaprine carries serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs, SNRIs, and tramadol; MAOIs are contraindicated.

whys.A: A baclofen withdrawal effect.
whys.C: Triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine.
whys.D: A G6PD/uricase concern.

takeaway: Cyclobenzaprine + SSRI/SNRI/tramadol → serotonin syndrome.
discriminator: Tizanidine’s interaction is CYP1A2; cyclobenzaprine’s is serotonergic.

stem: A runner sprained an ankle yesterday; the pain is sharp and clearly tied to the injury. How is this pain best classified by time course?

options.A: Neuropathic pain
options.B: Referred pain
options.C: Chronic pain
options.D: Phantom pain
options.E: Acute pain

why: Acute pain has recent onset and is often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.

whys.A: Neuropathic is a mechanism (nerve injury), not a time course.
whys.B: Not one of the lecture's categories.
whys.C: Chronic pain persists beyond expected healing time, often more than 3 months.
whys.D: Not one of the lecture's categories.

takeaway: Acute = recent and tied to an injury; chronic = beyond healing time, often > 3 months.
discriminator: Time course (acute vs. chronic) and mechanism (nociceptive, inflammatory, neuropathic) are two separate axes.

stem: A 70-year-old with knee OA has a flare limited to one knee despite acetaminophen and topical diclofenac. Which option does the lecture list for short-term relief?

options.A: Daily ketorolac for a month
options.B: Weekly oral methotrexate
options.C: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection
options.D: Infliximab infusion
options.E: High-dose hydroxychloroquine

why: Intra-articular corticosteroid injections give short-term relief for flares in a single joint.

whys.A: Ketorolac is short-term only.
whys.B: Methotrexate is a DMARD for RA.
whys.D: Biologics treat RA, not degenerative OA.
whys.E: Hydroxychloroquine is a DMARD for milder RA.

takeaway: OA ladder: acetaminophen → oral/topical NSAIDs → intra-articular steroid for a single-joint flare.
discriminator: OA tools are analgesic; RA tools are disease-modifying.
